AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a common disorder, and possibly underdiagnosed. In the elderly, OH has been considered a common cause of falls, fractures, and fear of falling. Its prevalence increases with age, probably related to the number of drug treatments, decreased fluid intake, and the progressive dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: To evaluate the prevalence of OH in a non-institutionalised population ≥80 years, according to different criteria based on sequential measurements taken at minute 0, 1, 3 and 5 of standing.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS DESIGN
AbstractText.content: A diagnostic accuracy study using an oscillometric device.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: Convenience sampling of 176 people ≥80 years attended in an urban Primary Health Care Centre.

AbstractText.Label: MEASUREMENTS
AbstractText.content: Supine and standing blood pressure (BP) measurements, at minutes 0, 1, 3 and 5 using the OMRON 705-CP blood pressure device. OH definition: decrease ≥20mmHg in systolic BP (SBP) and/or ≥10mmHg in diastolic BP (DBP).

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Mean age (Standard Deviation) was 85.2 (3.7) years, and 60.2% were women. Prevalence of OH: 30.7% at minute 0; 19.3% at minute 1; 18.2% at minute 3; and 20.5% at minute 5. Age, sedentary life, smoking, diabetes and SBP values were significantly associated with a greater BP decrease at minute 0.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: A third of the sample had OH, with a maximum prevalence at minute 0. From a clinical point of view, it is suggested that the definition of OH is prioritized according to the BP at minute 0.
